To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the performance of subjects on a verbal addition task is a function of the pre-experimental verbal set and the level of verbal noise to which they are exposed.

(1) the performance of subjects in a verbal addition task was affected by the presence or absence of a pre-experimental ‘set’; (2) the performance of the subjects was also affected by the presence of verbal noise; (3) the performance of those subjects who were given a pre-experimental set was not affected by the presence (or absence) of verbal noise; and (4) the performance of all subjects was affected by the absence of a preexperimental set.

(1) the effect of a noise level of 80 db on the performance of an arithmetic task is not significantly different from the effect of a quiet level of 40 db; (2) the effect of noise on performance of an arithmetic problem is not significantly different at two levels of difficulty, one easy and one difficult; (3) there is a significant difference between the effects of noise on two groups of subjects who differ in the extent to which they are able to concentrate their attention on the problem

the effect of noise upon the performance in a verbal addi tion task of a group of college students.
the effects of noise on the performance of verbal addition tasks by elementary school children.
two main areas: (1) the effects of noise on performance, and (2) the relationship between performance and pre-experimental ‘set’.

noise does not have a consistent and predictable influence on human performance, but that the evidence available does suggest the possibility that noise may be a significant variable in certain types of work.
there is a lack, at the present time, of conclusive evidence that noise has a significant effect on the work performance of adults.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the results are consistent with a theory of the effects of noise on human behavior which emphasizes the importance of the individual's pre-experimental ‘set’ as a determinant of the noise effects observed.
noise does have some effect on performance, and the effect varies with the type of task.

it has been shown that a high level of noise can be tolerated without any apparent loss in the ability of the subject to perform a verbal addition task, and that the performance of the subjects is not related to the level of noise.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we should all be aware that noise is a real issue and can have a significant impact on our health and well-being.
the noise of the environment is not a major factor in the performance of the task, and that the noise of a task is not a major cause of poor performance.
